case_study_insert.main_stem: Acacia Trails Safari Lodge (ATSL) is a cooperative in the hospitality and tourism sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 2011 by Sipho Dlamini, the lodge is owned and run by its staff-members and uses a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership, where staff vote on major decisions at monthly meetings. ATSL plans to invest $980,000 in a new tented eco-camp on adjacent land, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and a $380,000 member share issue. It has fixed costs of $4,970,000 a year, a variable cost of $88 a unit and a selling price of $230, and currently produces 46,000 units a year (one unit is one occupied guest-night). ATSL faces two problems: experienced safari guides are being poached by rival lodges, and absenteeism stands at 8%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary (October 2026): ATSL surveyed 540 recent guests; 71% would pay up to $30 more per guest-night for a tented eco-camp stay, and 84% named the guided wildlife experience as the lodge's strongest feature. Average occupancy is 66% against a target of 75%. Review scores average 8.8 out of 10 across 1,240 online reviews, and repeat guests generate 44% of annual bookings. Direct bookings via the lodge website rose 27% after a site relaunch. The worst-rated aspect was breakfast variety, mentioned in 18% of comments.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Acacia Trails Safari Lodge as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.0%, raising borrowing costs for the lodge's variable-rate ten-year bank loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.5% from $9.25 to $9.60 per hour from May 2026, lifting pay for lodge, catering and maintenance staff. (3) Diesel, park permit and laundry input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, while eco-tourism consumer spending in the region grew 6.8% in the same period.

questions.question_text: ATSL plans to finance part of its tented eco-camp expansion with a member share issue. Explain two advantages for ATSL of using a member share issue instead of a ten-year bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A member share issue raises $380,000 from the staff-owners themselves, with no interest to pay and no fixed repayment timetable, unlike the $600,000 ten-year bank loan. This protects ATSL's $4,970,000 fixed costs — already stretched by the 11.2% rise in diesel, park permit and laundry input costs and the 7.5% minimum wage increase — and means the cooperative is never at risk of default if tented eco-camp bookings start slowly at the 66% occupancy level.

Point 2: Share capital from members deepens commitment: staff-owners who buy in financially have a direct stake in the new camp's success, supporting the democratic culture at monthly meetings and reducing the risk of guides being poached, because leaving would mean giving up member status. No bank can seize ATSL's land or lodge if times are hard, and democratic control stays fully with members rather than passing to an outside lender imposing covenants.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Acacia Trails Safari Lodge and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: ATSL is launching its new tented eco-camp. Consider national newspaper advertising, social media influencer marketing, or exhibiting at a regional travel trade show. Which should ATSL choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National newspaper advertising: Major national papers would give ATSL broad awareness among potential eco-tourists across the country and suit a grand-opening story with beautiful photography of the tented camp. However, full-page colour rates are high for a cooperative with 85 employees funding $980,000 of expansion partly by bank loan, and papers reach a broad, untargeted audience including many people who will never book a safari; measured response rates for print advertising are weak.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with eco-travel and safari influencers targets exactly the 71% of surveyed past guests willing to pay up to $30 more per guest-night, uses the lodge's 8.8 review score and 1,240 reviews as persuasive proof, and produces measurable enquiries at low cost per reached viewer. It suits repeat and younger eco-tourists and amplifies the website's 27% direct-booking growth. Risks are influencer credibility and slower trust-building for luxury-price segments.

Travel trade show exhibition: A regional trade show puts ATSL directly in front of tour operators, corporate travel buyers and travel agents who package safari holidays, potentially securing group bookings and shoulder-season volume. Costs of stand space, travel and samples are moderate, and leads can be converted by follow-up. However, shows are episodic, reach a trade rather than consumer audience, and do little for direct repeat-guest marketing.

Recommendation: ATSL should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise eco-conscious segment identified in its research at the lowest cost per enquiry, leverages its 8.8/10 ratings and 44% repeat-guest base, and compounds with the website's direct bookings. Newspapers are rejected as too broad and expensive for the budget; the trade show is rejected as too narrow and episodic to fill the camp alone, though ATSL should attend one show a year to win operator contracts once the influencer campaign is live.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ATSL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ATSL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspaper advertising and the trade show are rejected.

questions.question_text: ATSL's experienced safari guides are being poached by rival lodges and absenteeism stands at 8%. Explain two benefits for ATSL of using job enrichment for its safari guides.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job enrichment gives guides greater responsibility — designing their own game-drive routes, leading guest safety briefings and mentoring junior staff — which satisfies their esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow) and raises the meaning of the work. Guides who feel trusted and challenged are far less likely to accept offers from rival lodges, directly reducing the poaching problem and the $4,970,000 cost pressure of repeatedly recruiting and certifying replacement guides.

Point 2: Enriched guides become more committed and proactive, improving the quality of the wildlife experience that 84% of surveyed guests rated as ATSL's strongest feature. They spot maintenance issues earlier, upsell the tented eco-camp and handle guest problems without escalation, supporting the 8.8 review score and 66% occupancy rate. Better motivation also tackles the 8% absenteeism directly, since staff with ownership over their role call in sick far less often than those doing repetitive, low-autonomy work. Enrichment is cheaper than across-the-board pay rises while the 7.5% minimum wage increase phases in, and it strengthens the cooperative's democratic culture, because empowered guides gain real influence rather than token consultation at monthly meetings.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ATSL's poaching problem, absenteeism and guest experience.

questions.question_text: ATSL must recruit two senior head guides for the new tented eco-camp. Consider recruiting externally from rival lodges or promoting and training existing junior guides from within the cooperative. Which should ATSL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External recruitment from rival lodges: Hiring already-proven head guides would bring immediate expertise, fresh ideas and established guest-handling skills, and could lift the tented camp's credibility from opening day; it also avoids the temporary productivity dip of internal promotion. However, rival-poached guides may carry rivals' habits rather than ATSL's democratic, community-owned values, would demand head-guide salaries well above existing internal rates, and — having been poached once themselves — may be poached again, recreating the exact instability ATSL is trying to solve.

Promoting and training existing junior guides: Internal promotion rewards the loyalty of members who built the lodge since 2011, costs less in salary shocks, and firmly strengthens democratic commitment and retention — the key defence against rival poaching. Training gaps can be closed with off-the-job courses, and the flat structure means promoted guides can genuinely influence tented-camp operations. The risks are a slower capability build-up, internal jealousy if the selection is not transparent, and the need to backfill the vacated junior roles.

Decision: ATSL should choose promoting and training existing junior guides. It directly counters the poaching problem, preserves cooperative culture and member trust at monthly meetings, and is far cheaper than market-rate external salaries at a time when the bank loan and share issue already commit $980,000. External recruitment is rejected because it imports flight risk and pay inflation; wholesale external hiring is only justified if no internal candidate meets the camp's guiding certification standard, which the interview data should be checked against first. A phased internal promotion, benchmarked against external salaries, keeps pay fair, transparent and defensible at the monthly members' meeting and signals to every junior guide that the cooperative invests in its own people.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two recruitment approaches with limited application to ATSL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both recruitment options in the context of ATSL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of ATSL with a well-justified decision covering cost, culture, retention and capability.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ATSL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $4,970,000 ÷ ($230 − $88) = $4,970,000 ÷ $142 = 35,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 35,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $230 − $88 = $142. Answer: contribution per unit is $142.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ATSL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. ATSL can compare the 35,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 46,000 guest-nights, a margin of safety of 11,000 units, to confirm the lodge trades above break-even and can service the $600,000 bank loan while the tented eco-camp ramps up toward the 75% occupancy target.
2. With $142 contribution per guest-night, management can test a direct-booking discount to nudge occupancy from 66% to 75% — for example a $20 reduction to $210 would cut contribution to $122 ($210 − $88) — and check whether added volume still covers the $4,970,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $4,970,000 and $142 contribution helps members set required guest-night targets for the new camp and decide how many tents to add each phase before spending the remaining budget from the $980,000 expansion.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($4,970,000 ÷ 46,000 units + $88 = $196.04 a unit) to compare the tented camp with the main lodge, identify whether catering (the 18% breakfast complaints) or laundry drives the 11.2% input-cost rise, and decide whether to renegotiate supplier contracts or add a breakfast surcharge.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 35,000 units a year, computed as $4,970,000 fixed costs divided by $142 contribution per guest-night (selling price $230 less variable cost $88). At the current 46,000-unit output, ATSL carries a margin of safety of 11,000 units, confirming the lodge trades comfortably above break-even while the tented eco-camp opens on adjacent land. (ii) Contribution per unit = $142 per occupied guest-night, the amount each guest-night adds toward fixed costs and then profit. (iii) Four applied uses: first, tracking the margin of safety toward the 75% occupancy target; second, modelling a $20 direct-booking discount that would cut contribution to $122 ($210 − $88) before any extra volume is gained; third, setting tented-camp rates and phase targets so the $980,000 expansion, financed by the $600,000 bank loan and $380,000 member share issue, stays above break-even; fourth, unit-cost benchmarking at $196.04 per guest-night ($4,970,000 ÷ 46,000 + $88) to expose catering and laundry overspends amid the 11.2% input-cost rise. Together these uses let Sipho Dlamini and the staff-members test whether camp-phase proposals and pricing decisions keep the lodge solvent through the shoulder seasons.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ATSL's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ATSL's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.68 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.77 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.23 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.37 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $140,000 inventories + $160,000 trade receivables + $220,000 cash = $520,000; 2025 current assets = $120,000 + $150,000 + $260,000 = $530,000. Current liabilities fell from $310,000 to $300,000. 2024: $520,000 ÷ $310,000 = 1.68; 2025: $530,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.77. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($520,000 − $140,000) ÷ $310,000 = $380,000 ÷ $310,000 = 1.23; 2025 = ($530,000 − $120,000) ÷ $300,000 = $410,000 ÷ $300,000 = 1.37.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. Current assets cover current liabilities more comfortably, and cash rose from $220,000 to $260,000 — a healthy cushion for a lodge whose occupancy is still only 66% and which is about to spend $980,000 on the tented eco-camp. The stricter measure rose from 1.23 to 1.37, so ATSL can meet short-term debts without selling food and beverage stock, a strength given the 11.2% rise in input costs. Cautions: trade receivables fell only marginally to $150,000, and any slow-paying corporate retreat bookings could tighten liquidity; current liabilities of $300,000 remain substantial against cash of $260,000, and the bank loan will add annual service charges from year one.

Conclusion: ATSL's financial position has improved. Both measures point to stronger short-term solvency in 2025, supported by lower inventories and lower liabilities. ATSL should protect this by keeping direct bookings growing, collecting agent commissions promptly and ring-fencing the eco-camp budget so the expansion does not erode the improved liquidity position.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether ATSL's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ATSL of opening the new tented eco-camp on adjacent land.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The tented eco-camp captures the 71% of surveyed guests willing to pay up to $30 more per guest-night for a tented experience, letting ATSL lift its $230 price point and its $142 contribution ($230 − $88) exactly where eco-tourism spending grew 6.8%. It uses the adjacent land efficiently, spreads fixed costs of $4,970,000 over more guest-nights, and gives ATSL a second product for the 44% repeat-guest base to try on their next stay, strengthening the 66% occupancy toward the 75% target.

Disadvantage: The camp commits $980,000 to new structures, equipment and access tracks before a single guest has stayed, financed partly by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan at a time when the base interest rate has just risen to 6.0%. If the camp launches slowly, its share of fixed costs and interest could outrun its revenue, diverting attention and maintenance capacity from the main lodge, damaging the 8.8 review score that carries ATSL's whole reputation, and straining the cooperative's democratic decision-making if members disagree on how fast to add tent phases.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ATSL's research, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 7.5% minimum wage increase to $9.60 and the 11.2% rise in diesel, park permit and laundry input costs will affect ATSL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.0%): If ATSL's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $4,500 a year in interest ($600,000 × 0.75% = $4,500), lifting fixed costs above $4,970,000. Higher rates also make discretionary eco-holidays slightly less tempting and would raise the cost of drawing down any remaining borrowing for the tented eco-camp. The absolute impact is the smallest of the three and can be managed by fixing the loan rate or by repaying early from member share capital, and unlike the other two factors it does not erode the $142 contribution ($230 − $88) per guest-night.

Minimum wage increase (7.5%, to $9.60 per hour from May 2026): Appendix 3 states both rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.35 ($9.60 − $9.25 = $0.35), the largest percentage rise of the three factors. The annual cost cannot be computed from the insert because the number of hours paid at the minimum wage is not stated; what can be shown is the break-even against the interest rise — the wage factor exceeds $4,500 once ATSL pays more than roughly 12,857 minimum-wage hours a year ($4,500 ÷ $0.35 ≈ 12,857 hours), a threshold comfortably exceeded by an 85-employee lodge with catering, laundry and maintenance staff. Because the lodge is a cooperative founded on fair member pay, absorbed wages are partly a governance commitment, not just an HR line item; compliance is non-negotiable and the 8% absenteeism makes any pay friction internally damaging.

Diesel, park permit and laundry input costs (up 11.2% year-on-year): Appendix 3 specifically names diesel, park permits and laundry — the exact running costs of game drives, guest access and linen service, all essential to a safari operation. No share of the $88 variable cost is stated, so the correct bound runs from $0 to an upper bound built on insert figures: applying the full 11.2% to the entire $88 gives at most about $9.86 per guest-night ($88 × 11.2% = $9.86), capping the damage at roughly $453,376 a year at the current 46,000 unit output (46,000 × $9.86). The true figure lies between the bounds; the insert permits no finer split, and any assumed share would be invented. What is certain is that these inputs recur on every game drive and every occupied room, concentrate in the $88 variable cost rather than in the $4,970,000 fixed costs, and cannot be switched to a cheaper park or laundered linens.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in diesel, park permit and laundry input costs will have the greatest impact. It is the steepest percentage increase named in Appendix 3, recurrences on every one of 46,000 guest-nights, escapes refinancing, and — unlike the wage factor, whose cash effect is limited to minimum-wage hours at $0.35 each — applies to all consumption regardless of who delivers it. Supplier renegotiation, route efficiencies, on-site laundry for the tented eco-camp and selective price increases (71% of surveyed guests accept up to $30 more per night) are the levers ATSL must pull; the 7.5% wage rise is the second serious pressure in an 85-member cooperative already fighting poaching, and the $4,500 interest-rate effect is the smallest of the three and can be neutralised by fixing the loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ATSL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ATSL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ATSL with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
